name: Preparation H under eyes

lead: Some people dab Preparation H, a hemorrhoid product, under the eyes as a beauty hack, reasoning that its blood-vessel constrictor will temporarily shrink puffiness and bags.

Some versions contain 0.25% phenylephrine, a vasoconstrictor, and shark liver oil; others use 1% hydrocortisone, pramoxine, witch hazel or caffeine, and formulations differ by country. Proponents point to the phenylephrine as the active mechanism: narrower vessels, less swelling. No study of the product on periorbital skin was found, and it is labelled for hemorrhoids.

paras: Posters describe dabbing a thin layer under the eyes, avoiding the lash line, usually shortly before an event, and wiping it off after a while. It is used as an occasional off-label trick rather than a routine.

The product is made for anorectal use, not eyelids. Dermatology references note that medications causing rebound after vasoconstrictors can darken the area, and steroid versions raise skin-thinning concerns. No safety data for periorbital use were found.

angle.text: Users dab the hemorrhoid product Preparation H under the eyes off-label, believing its vasoconstrictor shrinks under-eye vessels and temporarily reduces bags and puffiness. No studies of this use were found.

lead: Preparation H under eyes is an off-label practice in which the hemorrhoid product Preparation H is dabbed on the skin beneath the eyes to reduce puffiness and bags, so the area looks smoother and more rested. It circulates in beauty lore and appearance communities as a quick, pharmacy-counter de-puffing trick.

Preparation H is an American brand now owned by Pfizer, sold as gels, ointments, suppositories and wipes. Active ingredients vary by country and include phenylephrine, hydrocortisone, pramoxine, witch hazel and caffeine, and some versions contain shark liver oil or yeast extract [1]. Proponents point to phenylephrine, which constricts blood vessels, as the ingredient that tightens the swollen under-eye area; phenylephrine is a selective alpha-1 adrenergic agonist that narrows arteries and veins and is used at about 0.25 percent in hemorrhoid products to shrink swollen veins [2].

No published study has tested the product on periorbital skin, and its labelled use is anorectal. Dermatology references on dark circles note that thin eyelid skin shows underlying features and that rebound after vasoconstrictors can darken the area [3].
infobox: Phenylephrine 0.25%, hydrocortisone, pramoxine, witch hazel, caffeine

paras: The original formulation was developed by inventor George Sperti with a yeast extract as the main ingredient. American Home Products acquired a sunburn oil in 1935 that became Preparation H, the company was renamed Wyeth in 2002, and Pfizer bought Wyeth in 2009 [1]. A yeast extract component was removed from the US formulation in 1995 but remains in some other countries, such as Canada, where the manufacturer says the extract smooths wrinkles and soothes dry, irritated skin [1]. Formulations differ between countries [1].

Believers say phenylephrine constricts the small vessels beneath thin eyelid skin and reduces swelling. In its medical uses phenylephrine narrows blood vessels, which is why it appears in hemorrhoid products and in eye drops that dilate the pupil [2]. Whether the product has a visible effect on the periorbital area has not been tested. Dermatology references describe rebound vasodilation after vasoconstrictors as a possible contributor to darkened skin [3].

The product is labelled for anorectal use. Formulations containing hydrocortisone are corticosteroids, and eyelid skin is thin. Phenylephrine's documented adverse effects relate to systemic exposure and include raised blood pressure and heart rhythm effects, and it is avoided in people with hypertension, heart disease or narrow-angle glaucoma [2]. No data describe these risks for under-eye application.
No studies found for use under the eyes. A 1984 study examined the product's effect on wound healing in the human rectum, which does not address appearance [4].
